19. **The living map.** (added 29 October 2026) Haakon: "In time I want environmental effects, seasons reflected on the map. Characters, armies, fighting shown, etc. Everything you can think of, which makes it a better game for a player or viewer. But I don't believe the time for these effects are quiet yet." With every feature built, the map's look becomes a blend of Imperator: Rome's map and a museum map of the Bronze Age world ("The map in true geography, and its look in time" under Interface): the environment and the seasons on the map, characters, armies and battles as they travel and fight, every unit and figure drawn after the period's own relics in its culture's idiom, a map that remembers the war, life drawn from the simulation, every level of what is built (roads by quality, harbours and docks, walls, water works, granaries, mines), a seasonal year, each realm's own map drawn by its scribes, omens in the margin and small scenes at big moments, and whatever else makes the game better to play or to watch, each measured on a throttled phone. Presentation only, with no change to rules, numbers or balance, so it may run beside item 18. **Stop for review.** Then **19+, answers to 19's review** (30 October 2026; Haakon: "Yes to all"): each realm's own map pressed in clay for every court that writes cuneiform, as the period's clay maps were, and on papyrus for Egypt; a sacked city stays in ruins until its people come back, and they come back by the rule that already moves them ("Feeding a province draws its people": settled people move towards more room, measured in food, and the loose drift towards richer land), so the ruins fade as its people return and its walls are rebuilt with item 15's works, with no rule for rebuilding (Haakon: "no special rules for cities recovering, people will migrate back at the harvest potential difference there becomes bigger than neighboring cities"); and Egypt's view gets hieratic notes as decoration only, the map's own text staying in the reader's language. Presentation only.
